body_text: The American consumer is exhausted and enraged by rising prices, and ready, according to consumer data, to spend a $1 billion on packaged food that’s labeled “seed-oil free.” Seed oils are, of course, the fashionable, if scientifically dubious, boogeyman. Data doesn’t back up claims of various health harms caused by seed oils but the Americans aren’t letting that get in the way: seed-oil-free products saw a 72% gain compared to a year earlier, and sales of seed-oil-free salty snacks climbed 87%, compared to just 2.9% for products without the label, Bloomberg News reported based on NIQ data. Big food companies like PepsiCo and ConAgra are making the switch by relying on olive and avocado oil. Markets bounced back Monday, rising after last week’s AI-trade induced wipeout, despite news over the weekend about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy (more on that story below.) “We’ve spent all this time worrying about AI cybersecurity risks when our true vulnerabilities come from human frailty,” was how Entrypoint’s Luke Kawa summed it up . On Sunday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang released a statement admitting to an extra-marital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang’s statement comes after the New York Times first reported on the CEO’s “close” relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le. American officials, the NYT reported, had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset and involved in helping China evade constraints limiting its ability to import high-powered AI chips. Nvidia’s board of directors has opened an investigation into Huang’s conduct but has said it does not believe US national security or its own intellectual property have been compromised. The specifics don’t look good: Alice Huang is the CEO of Megaspeed , a Singapore-based data center company that has been an absolutely massive buyer of Nvidia chips. She is believed by US intelligence officials to have been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS), the Financial Times reported . The MSS fulfills a role similar to a combination of the CIA, FBI, and NSA. The US Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions that it was buying Nvidia AI chips in order to smuggle them into China before the probe was suddenly called off and transferred to the Justice Department late last year, the New York Times reported Monday . That switch came after Nvidia’s general counsel emailed Commerce Department investigators seeking information about the inquiry. Other tech stocks surged on Monday – the PHLX Semiconductor index gained almost 7% despite Nvdia falling about 4.5% on the day. As Kawa pointed out in yesterday’s Entrypoint newsletter, the market has for months now been a bit skeptical about the medium-term outlook for Nvdia’s profits. If you assume the chip giant’s quarter-on-quarter earnings-per-share growth dips to less than half its current average and investors give the stock a valuation in its recent lowest quartile, Kawa ballparks that Nvidia would be worth… about what it is today. Score one for the strong-form efficient markets hypothesis , I guess. At the same time, it’s hard exactly to know how Jensen Huang will respond to being put under a very new kind of public spotlight, and whether investors will have confidence in anyone but him to deliver the kind of returns he has overseen. title: 🎓 Midterms Studying
body_text: Sometimes it’s important to remember what sport you’re playing, as recently a hard-fought Brazilian youth soccer game devolved into a piqued MLB game or relatively subdued and reasonable ice hockey game. The game became a brawl that resulted in a world-record 53 red cards that ejected 43 players, 8 coaches, and two team board members from the fight on the field. In any company, it’s always nice to know the board has got your back, I guess. On Friday, stocks rebounded somewhat from Thursday’s $2.5T Nasdaq bloodbath, but overall finished a volatile week in the red. Last week the midterms resulted in a sweeping victory for congressional Democrats, and in the days that followed it became clear that what that means for the market is obvious, uncomplicated, and straightforward: nobody really knows exactly what that meant for the market, it’s very complicated and in no way straightforward. The day after the midterms stocks surged, the day after that the Nasdaq took a historic dump, and then the day after that things bounced back a bit. The upshot of last week in the aggregate was down a bit, but sector-by-sector things are not so simple. Companies used the opportunity of the market chaos to rip off some band-aids. Microsoft made a flurry of announcements that amounted to a paring back deals with the external providers of compute — chastising the neoclouds and pulling the plug on a compute rental provided by Oracle — that certainly sent a chill through the parts of the AI trade that serve those interests. Tesla managed to pop 5% on Friday in a week that was, electorally speaking, a fundamental rejection of the political project of Elon Musk. It did so by announcing that it was going to stop bleeding money out making Cybertrucks, and instead throw those production lines towards making Cybercabs. There was lots of more general house cleaning, such as Waymo announcing it would soon soon be done working with Uber , Oracle canceling a chip lease agreement with Tencent, Kraft Heinz planning to sell off its coffee business, and CVS spinning off… CVS. All the kind of news you drop when the market is so crazy you can’t really figure out what’s moving what. In all, the week was less about the end of this trade or the start of that, but more of a rotation. Hyperscalers Microsoft, Amazon and Google all finished the week up; if the week revealed anything, it’s that having existing datacenters in the ground is important, and that if you’re a company planning on putting more in the ground, well, maybe you should let Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa save you from yourself, and just go ahead and give that money to shareholders instead. Meanwhile, some of the biggest losers of the week were the companies that were riding the high of those companies capex moves. Some of the biggest drops of the week were storage chips ( Seagate , Sandisk ) and the connectivity and so-called “picks-and-shovels” of the data center build-out ( Lumentum , Marvell , Astera Labs , Micron ). Speaking of picks and shovels, another trade indicates how the midterms’ pushback on new data center construction has manifested in markets. Sure, companies like Caterpillar dropped, but homebuilders gained. Caterpillar supplies the literal picks and shovels of the data center build-out, and with that potentially slowing down, so did it. On the other hand, homebuilders that have had an exhausting time competing with data center construction for capital, materials, and labor surged, with Toll Brothers , DR Horton and PulteGroup all finishing the week up. A nota bene on PulteGroup that shows how weird this market has been. The large residential construction company was a huge winner of the week, spiking 8% between Tuesday's close and Wednesday's open, finishing the week up nearly 5%, now that Democrats will finally have a hand in steering housing policy. This is a somewhat ironic market rebuke of the administration, given that the grandson of the company's founder is currently serving as Trump's director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency and head of Freddie Mac. My colleague Luke Kawa, who writes the brilliant EntryPoint newsletter that goes in-depth on this stuff, is fond of the aphorism “my capex spending is your profit margins,” and that has been on display this past week. The AI trade will continue, but the beneficiaries of that trade — and the ultimate total addressable market of the business — will remain in flux. A few weeks ago, we wrote about the CoreWeave debt contretemps, and we made the point that just because a company got a lot of money doesn’t mean it’s gonna be one of the winners of the AI trade, writing “Just because your business model was the beating heart of the AI industry in 2026 doesn’t prevent you from being the bloated, doomed appendix of the AI industry in 2032. Not every buzzy well-funded company’s gonna make it.” Last week, if anything, confirmed that the future indeed won’t be evenly distributed. Okay, Uber might have been a “ little bit of a crapshoot ” for riders looking to book a robotaxi, per Waymo’s co-CEO. Yes, notching just four ride bookings via AI agents during the Halloween period probably wasn’t the spooky season performance it had hoped for. And alright, the company’s president defecting to OpenAI might have added to what hasn’t, on the surface, been a great news week for Uber. Park all of that for just a minute, however, and some of the numbers out of Uber’s third-quarter report earlier this week must still have been enough for execs still at the company to cheer at least a little. Although revaluing equity investments weighed on earnings to the point of missing, Uber revenues rose 9.6% from last year to hit $14.77 billion and beat estimates. Trips taken on Uber — that is, slightly confusingly, the sum of trips taken in Uber cars and total deliveries made on Uber Eats — hit a staggering 4.06 billion in the quarter. That tally means that each of Uber’s 215 million monthly active platform users must have ordered a taxi, or a taxi for their burrito , just shy of 19 times (more than six times each month) on average last quarter. Imagine how many more the company could’ve clocked without the driver shortages in India, Canada, and Brazil that it also disclosed this quarter . For those of you who see that trip figure and still assume Uber mostly functions as a ride-hailing service, the company’s split on gross bookings, which rose 20% from last year to reach almost $60 billion in the third quarter, might not be what you expect… and the balance might not have been how you thought for a while now. Since Delivery gross bookings value overtook Mobility during the pandemic era — remember? Not many of us were taking taxis and a lot of us were getting stuff delivered because there was nothing else to do? — there’s really not been a huge margin separating the two in either direction. In the last quarter, Uber booked $29.5 billion from rides and just around $1 billion less from its Delivery segment; its Freight division, which brought in $1.8 billion, still clearly has a ways to go. While some of the more eye-catching Uber news this week might not have looked great on paper, the billions of trips and hundreds of millions of riders and users that the company notches each quarter undoubtedly softened the blow.
